Missions.title: Let's start teaching Pixy simple things!
Missions.subtitle: choose a topic to teach:

Quiz.title: Quiz
Quiz.introTitle: Let's see what you know about AI!
Quiz.introSubtitle: This is just a quick introduction to understand your knowledge.
Quiz.resultHelperText: Nice work! You can review each question and see the correct answers.
Quiz.resultHelperTextHigh: Outstanding! Open the breakdown below to see each question.
Quiz.resultHelperTextMid: Solid progress! Review what you missed to lock it in.
Quiz.resultHelperTextLow: Every try counts. Check the correct answers below and keep going!
Quiz.missionHintLine: Tap an answer, then continue to learn why it matters.
Quiz.reviewSubtitle: Your picks compared with the correct answers.
Quiz.lessonCard1Body: Artificial Intelligence is when computers learn to solve problems on their own. Instead of following step-by-step rules for everything, an AI program discovers patterns in data and uses them to make decisions — a bit like how you learn to ride a bike by practicing, not by reading a manual.
Quiz.lessonCard1Fact: The term "Artificial Intelligence" was invented in 1956 — that's before your grandparents had computers at home!
Quiz.lessonCard2Body: AI needs data the way a chef needs ingredients. To recognize dogs, it looks at millions of dog photos. To translate languages, it reads billions of sentences. The quality and amount of data determine how well AI can learn — garbage in, garbage out!
Quiz.lessonCard2Fact: GPT models trained on text from over 8 million web pages — that's more reading than any human could do in a thousand lifetimes!
Quiz.lessonCard3Body: AI is hiding in your daily life! Spam filters protect your email, maps find the fastest route home, video games create smart enemies, and cameras on phones recognize your face. Even autocorrect on your keyboard is a tiny AI!
Quiz.lessonCard3Fact: Netflix saves about $1 billion a year because its AI recommends shows you actually want to watch, so fewer people cancel!
Quiz.lessonCard4Body: AI can beat world champions at chess and Go, write stories, compose music, and create art. But it doesn't understand what it's doing — it finds statistical patterns without feeling, dreaming, or being curious. It has no awareness, no emotions, and no wishes.
Quiz.lessonCard4Fact: In 2016, Google's AlphaGo beat the world champion at Go — a game so complex it has more possible moves than atoms in the universe!
Quiz.lessonCard5Body: AI is a powerful tool, but it's people who decide how to use it. It can help doctors find diseases earlier, scientists protect endangered animals, and students learn at their own pace. The choices we make today shape the AI of tomorrow — and your generation will lead the way!
Quiz.lessonCard5Fact: AI is already helping rangers in Africa track and protect rhinos from poachers using camera traps and image recognition!

Animals.lookAtImage: Look at this image and think about what you see in it.
Animals.lessonCard1Body: Pixy uses something called a neural network to recognize animals. Think of it like a brain made of math! It has millions of tiny connections that work together. When Pixy looks at a photo, these connections light up in different patterns for cats, dogs, elephants, and more.
Animals.lessonCard1Fact: The neural network Pixy uses (called MobileNetV2) has over 3 million connections — but it can still run on your phone!
Animals.lessonCard2Body: Pixy didn't start from scratch! It already learned to recognize thousands of things — from cars to flowers — by studying millions of photos. This is called transfer learning. Instead of learning everything over again, Pixy reused what it already knew and focused on the 5 animals you taught it.
Animals.lessonCard2Fact: Transfer learning lets AI learn new tasks 10x faster — just like how knowing how to ride a bike helps you learn to ride a motorcycle!
Animals.lessonCard3Body: When Pixy says 'I'm 85% sure this is a cat', it's showing its confidence. The AI calculates a score for each animal and picks the highest one. High confidence means the patterns strongly match one animal. Low confidence means the image could be several things.
Animals.lessonCard3Fact: Doctors use AI confidence scores to decide when to trust a computer's diagnosis and when a human expert should double-check!
Animals.lessonCard4Body: At first, Pixy made lots of mistakes — confusing dogs with cats or horses with elephants. But every time you taught Pixy the right answer, its skill level went up! This is like adjusting the 'temperature' of Pixy's brain: at low skill it guesses wildly, at high skill it uses its real knowledge.
Animals.lessonCard4Fact: Real AI models improve the same way — companies like Tesla collect millions of driving examples to make self-driving cars smarter every day!
Animals.lessonCard5Title: AI for Animals in the Real World
Animals.lessonCard5Body: The same technology Pixy uses helps protect real animals! Scientists place cameras in forests and use AI to automatically identify species — from rare snow leopards to tiny frogs. AI can count animals, track their movements, and alert rangers when poachers are near.
Animals.lessonCard5Fact: Microsoft's AI for Earth program has helped identify over 30,000 species using image recognition — the same kind of AI you just used with Pixy!

Drawing.title: Draw a Blue Triangle
Drawing.subtitle: Creative Mission
Drawing.instruction: Draw a triangle using blue color! Tap the canvas to start drawing. 🎨
Drawing.thinking: Hmm, let me look at your drawing... 🤔
Drawing.successMessage: You drew a perfect blue triangle!
Drawing.wrongColorHint: Don't forget to use blue color! Look at the color palette! 🎨
Drawing.captureError: Could not capture drawing. Try again!
Drawing.drawPromptPart3: color! Tap the canvas to start. 🎨
Drawing.colorCircleInstruction: Color the circle using RED! Stay inside the lines! 🎨
Drawing.colorCircleThinking: Hmm, let me check your coloring... 🤔
Drawing.shapesLessonCard1Body: When you drew a shape, Pixy didn't just 'look' at it like you do. It converted your drawing into a grid of tiny numbers (pixels) and used math to find the edges and outlines. This is called computer vision — teaching computers to understand images!
Drawing.shapesLessonCard1Fact: Self-driving cars use computer vision to read road signs, spot pedestrians, and stay in their lane — all in real time!
Drawing.shapesLessonCard2Body: Pixy found your shape by detecting its contour — the outline where your drawing meets the background. It uses a technique called thresholding: everything darker than a certain level becomes 'drawing', everything lighter becomes 'paper'. Then it traces the boundary!
Drawing.shapesLessonCard2Fact: Doctors use contour detection to outline tumors in medical scans, helping them measure size and plan treatments more accurately!
Drawing.shapesLessonCard3Body: Every shape has a mathematical 'fingerprint' called Hu Moments. A circle's fingerprint is different from a triangle's, no matter how big, small, or rotated it is! Pixy compares your drawing's fingerprint against reference shapes to figure out what you drew.
Drawing.shapesLessonCard3Fact: Hu Moments were invented in 1962 by Ming-Kuei Hu and are still used today in robotics, satellite imagery, and handwriting recognition!
Drawing.shapesLessonCard4Body: Pixy doesn't rely on just one method! It uses four different strategies to identify your shape, and they all vote together. Hu Moments check the mathematical fingerprint, circularity measures roundness, contour features look at proportions, and Fourier descriptors analyze the shape's frequency pattern. The shape with the most votes wins!
Drawing.shapesLessonCard4Fact: This 'voting' approach is called ensemble learning — it's the same idea behind weather forecasts that combine multiple models to give better predictions!
Drawing.shapesLessonCard5Title: Computer Vision in the Real World
Drawing.shapesLessonCard5Body: The same shape recognition technology Pixy uses helps robots pick up objects on factory lines, lets your phone scan documents by detecting page edges, and powers augmented reality apps that overlay graphics onto real-world surfaces. Computer vision is everywhere!
Drawing.shapesLessonCard5Fact: NASA uses computer vision to analyze photos from Mars rovers — the AI identifies rocks, craters, and safe paths automatically!
Drawing.colorLessonCard1Body: You see 'red' or 'blue', but a computer sees three numbers for every tiny dot (pixel) in your drawing: how much Red, Green, and Blue light to mix. This is called RGB. By combining different amounts, a computer can represent millions of colors — and Pixy analyzes each pixel to understand what colors you used!
Drawing.colorLessonCard1Fact: The human eye can distinguish about 10 million colors, but a computer screen with RGB can display over 16 million different combinations!
Drawing.colorLessonCard2Body: Instead of checking every single pixel, Pixy groups similar colors together using a smart algorithm called K-Means. Imagine dumping all your colored pixels on a table and sorting them into 3 piles by similarity. The biggest pile is your main color! This is much more reliable than checking one pixel at a time.
Drawing.colorLessonCard2Fact: K-Means was invented in 1957 and is used everywhere — from compressing images on websites to grouping customers in marketing!
Drawing.colorLessonCard3Body: Pixy converts colors from RGB to HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value). Hue is the actual color (red, blue, green), Saturation is how vivid it is, and Value is how bright. HSV is much better for recognizing colors because a 'dark red' and 'bright red' have similar Hue even though their RGB numbers look very different.
Drawing.colorLessonCard3Fact: Artists have used the HSV color wheel for centuries! The digital version just turned their intuition into math that computers can use.
Drawing.colorLessonCard4Body: Before analyzing colors, Pixy needs to know which pixels are your drawing and which are just the white paper. It checks the corners of the image (which are almost always background), figures out the background color, and ignores those pixels. This way it only looks at the colors YOU drew!
Drawing.colorLessonCard4Fact: The same background detection technique helps video calls blur or replace your background — the AI separates 'you' from 'room' in real time!
Drawing.colorLessonCard5Title: Color AI in the Real World
Drawing.colorLessonCard5Body: Color detection AI is used in amazing ways! Farmers use it to check if fruits are ripe by analyzing their color from drone photos. Fashion apps match your outfit colors automatically. Quality control in factories detects products with wrong colors. Even wildlife researchers identify bird species by their unique feather patterns!
Drawing.colorLessonCard5Fact: Pantone, the company that defines official colors, now uses AI to predict trending colors for next year's fashion — analyzing millions of images from social media!

GroupingSorting.title: Group the Images
GroupingSorting.subtitle: Sort items into the correct categories
GroupingSorting.instruction: Drag each image into the correct category
GroupingSorting.tapSubmitHint: Tap Submit to check your answers
GroupingSorting.masteredMessage:
You mastered the grouping challenge!
Pixy is impressed! 🌟
GroupingSorting.lessonCard1Body: You just sorted images into groups like 'fruits' and 'vegetables'! This is exactly what AI does — it's called classification. When you see an apple, your brain instantly knows it's a fruit. AI learns to do the same thing by studying thousands of labeled examples until it can sort new items on its own.
GroupingSorting.lessonCard1Fact: Gmail's spam filter classifies over 100 million spam emails every day — sorting them away from your inbox automatically!
GroupingSorting.lessonCard2Title: Features — How AI Tells Things Apart
GroupingSorting.lessonCard2Body: How did you decide a carrot is a vegetable? You looked at its shape, color, and what you know about it. AI does something similar — it finds 'features' in each image: edges, colors, textures, and patterns. These features become a fingerprint that helps AI decide which category something belongs to.
GroupingSorting.lessonCard2Fact: AI can detect over 1,000 different features in a single image — far more than the human eye consciously notices!
GroupingSorting.lessonCard3Body: AI learning has two phases: training and prediction. During training, AI sees many labeled examples (like your grouping exercise) and learns the rules. During prediction, AI uses those rules to classify new items it has never seen before. The more training examples, the better the predictions!
GroupingSorting.lessonCard3Fact: Modern AI models are trained on datasets with millions of images — but they can then classify a new image in less than a millisecond!
GroupingSorting.lessonCard4Body: After sorting, you saw which items you got right and wrong. AI scientists use a tool called a 'confusion matrix' to track the same thing — it shows where the AI gets confused between categories. If an AI keeps mixing up tomatoes and apples (both round and red!), the confusion matrix reveals it so engineers can improve the model.
GroupingSorting.lessonCard4Fact: The confusion matrix was invented in 1904 by Karl Pearson — over 100 years before modern AI, but it's still one of the most important tools in machine learning!
GroupingSorting.lessonCard5Title: Sorting AI in the Real World
GroupingSorting.lessonCard5Body: The same grouping logic AI uses is everywhere! Recycling plants use AI to sort plastic, glass, and metal. Post offices sort millions of letters by reading handwritten addresses. Music apps classify songs by genre. Even hospitals sort medical images to help doctors find the right diagnosis faster.
GroupingSorting.lessonCard5Fact: Amazon's warehouses use AI-powered robots that classify and sort over 1 million packages per day — each one placed in the right bin automatically!

PixyLearns.introBody: Help Pixy understand the world by teaching it to recognize different things. Label the images and watch Pixy learn!
PixyLearns.teachPixyHint: Tap each image and select the correct label
PixyLearns.aiExplanation: This is how AI learns! By seeing many examples, Pixy can now tell the difference between apples and cats.
PixyLearns.lessonCard1Body: You just taught Pixy to tell apples apart from cats! This is called image classification — one of the first things AI learns to do. Just like you can instantly recognize a cat or an apple, AI learns to sort images into categories by studying lots of examples.
PixyLearns.lessonCard1Fact: Image classification AI can sort through thousands of photos per second — way faster than any human could!
PixyLearns.lessonCard2Body: The labeled images you gave Pixy are called training data. Every time you tapped 'Apple' or 'Cat', you gave Pixy an example to learn from. The more examples AI gets, the better it becomes at recognizing new images it has never seen before.
PixyLearns.lessonCard2Fact: Google Photos uses training data from billions of images to recognize faces, pets, and places in your photo library!
PixyLearns.lessonCard3Body: When a human teaches AI by showing it the correct answers — like you did with Pixy — it's called supervised learning. You were the supervisor! Without your labels, Pixy would just see random pixels and have no idea what anything is.
PixyLearns.lessonCard3Fact: The word 'supervised' comes from the Latin word meaning 'to watch over' — and that's exactly what you did for Pixy!
PixyLearns.lessonCard4Body: AI doesn't see pictures the way you do. It sees a grid of tiny colored dots called pixels. It looks for patterns — shapes, edges, colors, textures — to figure out what's in the image. A cat has pointy ears and whiskers; an apple is round and red or green.
PixyLearns.lessonCard4Fact: A single smartphone photo has over 12 million pixels — and AI analyzes every one of them to understand what it's looking at!
PixyLearns.lessonCard5Title: AI Vision in the Real World
PixyLearns.lessonCard5Body: The same technology you used to teach Pixy is used everywhere! Doctors use it to spot diseases in X-rays, farmers use it to check if fruits are ripe, and self-driving cars use it to see roads and traffic signs. Your phone even uses it for face unlock and photo filters!
PixyLearns.lessonCard5Fact: AI image recognition helps scientists count endangered animals in wildlife photos — saving thousands of hours of manual work!

About.title: About Thinky
About.missionBody: Thinky is an interactive, educational, gamified app for children ages 7–12. Through games and the mascot Pixy, kids learn the basics of artificial intelligence. Along the way, the mascot is “trained” by the child, echoing how real machine-learning models learn from examples.
About.objective1: Introduce AI ideas in a friendly, intuitive way.
About.objective2: Simulate a simple model that improves from the child’s interactions.
About.objective3: Use an animated mascot as a guide, partner, and learning model.

Help.title: Help & FAQ
Help.faqSubtitle: Find answers to the most common questions about Thinky.
Help.faq1Q: What is Thinky and who is it for?
Help.faq1A: Thinky is an educational app for children ages 7–12. It teaches the basics of artificial intelligence through interactive games and by training the mascot Pixy.
Help.faq2Q: How does the Pixy mascot work?
Help.faq2A: Pixy is your digital mascot that “learns” from your interactions. As you complete missions and give feedback, Pixy simulates how an AI model improves from examples. You can also chat with Pixy in the assistant tab.
Help.faq3Q: What are missions and how do I earn XP?
Help.faq3A: Missions are educational games about AI: images, colors, shapes, animals, vocabulary, and more. Completing quizzes earns XP based on your score. The leaderboard ranks players by total XP.
Help.faq4A: The Workshop is where you explore missions made by others or create your own. Download new missions to learn and play community quizzes.
Help.faq5A: The leaderboard ranks players by total XP earned from quizzes. Stats such as player count and average XP reflect the whole community.
Help.faq6Q: Can I use the app without an account?
Help.faq6A: Yes. You can play as a guest with just a name; progress is stored on the device. Create an account to sync across devices and join the leaderboard.
Help.faq7Q: How do I change the language?
Help.faq7A: Go to Profile → Settings → Language and choose English or Română. The change applies immediately across the app.
Help.faq8Q: The app does not load correctly. What should I do?
Help.faq8A: Check your internet connection. If you use a development build, ensure the backend is running. Try restarting the app or clearing the app cache.
